zeta.context: The lowercase Greek letter zeta, a short top bar that runs into a steep curve and a small tail. Used for the Riemann zeta function, damping ratios in engineering and as a variable in math and physics.

eta-letter.context: The lowercase Greek letter eta, drawn as an n whose right stem drops below the line. Used for efficiency, viscosity and learning rate in formulas across physics, engineering and machine learning.

xi.context: The lowercase Greek letter xi, a stack of curls under a short top bar with a hooked tail. Seen in statistics, physics and advanced math as a variable or random quantity.

rho.context: The lowercase Greek letter rho, a round bowl with a straight stem dropping from its left side. Used for density, resistivity and correlation coefficients in science and statistics.

tau.context: The lowercase Greek letter tau, a top bar with one stem that curls to the right at its foot. Used for torque, time constants, shear stress and the circle constant equal to two pi.

chi.context: The lowercase Greek letter chi, a tall cross whose one stroke bends in a gentle S and dips below the line. Best known from the chi squared test in statistics and from susceptibility in physics.

psi.context: The Greek letter psi, a cup crossed by a tall stem like a trident. Used for the wave function in quantum mechanics, for pounds per square inch and as a symbol of psychology.

kappa-letter.context: The lowercase Greek letter kappa, a short upright stem with two diagonal arms like a compact k. Used for curvature, thermal conductivity and the kappa statistic for agreement.

aleph.context: The Hebrew letter aleph, a slanted stroke with one arm up on the right and one leg down on the left. In set theory aleph numbers measure the sizes of infinite sets.

h-bar.context: An italic h with a short bar across its tall stem, the reduced Planck constant. Written throughout quantum mechanics, from the uncertainty principle to the Schrodinger equation.

partial-derivative.context: The partial derivative sign, a round bowl with a stroke that curls up and over to the left like a backward 6. Used in multivariable calculus, physics and machine learning gradients.

double-integral.context: Two tall integral signs side by side, the notation for integrating over a region of a plane. Used for areas, volumes under surfaces and averages in two dimensions.

triple-integral.context: Three slender integral signs side by side, the notation for integrating over a solid region in space. Used for volume, mass and charge in three dimensions.

contour-integral.context: An integral sign threaded through a small circle, meaning integration around a closed path. Common in complex analysis, electromagnetism and fluid flow.

absolute-value.context: A letter x between two tall vertical bars, the absolute value or modulus of a number. Means the distance from zero with the sign removed, also used for vector length.

floor-function.context: An x held between two brackets that have only bottom feet, the floor function. It rounds a number down to the nearest whole number and appears in math and programming.

proportional-to.context: The proportional-to sign, a sideways loop that opens to the right. Written between two quantities that grow or shrink together at a fixed ratio.

congruent.context: The congruence sign, a tilde above two parallel bars. Says that two shapes are identical in size and shape, and in algebra that two structures are isomorphic.

similar-to.context: A small triangle and a larger triangle under a tilde, the sign for similar figures. Shapes that are similar have the same angles and proportions but different sizes.

perpendicular.context: An upright line standing on a base line with a small square in the corner, the perpendicular sign. Marks lines or planes that meet at a right angle.

parallel-lines-symbol.context: Two slanted parallel strokes side by side, the sign for parallel lines. Written between two lines that never meet, and sometimes for parallel circuits.

arc-notation.context: The capital letters A and B under a curved arc, the notation for the arc between two points on a circle. Used in geometry lessons and circle theorems.

line-segment-notation.context: The capital letters A and B under a straight bar, the notation for the line segment joining two points. Used in geometry to name a segment and its length.

natural-numbers.context: A blackboard bold capital N with a doubled left stem, the symbol for the set of natural numbers. These are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and onward, sometimes with 0.

integers-set.context: A blackboard bold capital Z with a doubled diagonal, the symbol for the set of integers. Covers all whole numbers, positive, negative and zero.

rational-numbers.context: A blackboard bold capital Q with a doubled inner stroke and a tail, the symbol for the set of rational numbers. These are all numbers that can be written as a fraction of integers.

real-numbers.context: A blackboard bold capital R with a doubled stem, the symbol for the set of real numbers. Includes every point on the number line, rational and irrational.

complex-numbers.context: A blackboard bold capital C with a doubled inner stroke, the symbol for the set of complex numbers. These combine a real part and an imaginary part.

logical-not.context: The logical negation sign, a horizontal bar with a short hook down at its right end. Placed before a statement to mean it is not true, in logic and boolean algebra.

implies.context: A double-stroke arrow pointing right, the implication sign. Means if the statement on the left is true then the one on the right is too, in logic and proofs.

if-and-only-if.context: A double-stroke arrow with heads at both ends, the biconditional sign. Means two statements are logically equivalent, each one true exactly when the other is.

maps-to.context: A right-pointing arrow that starts from a short vertical bar, the maps-to sign. Shows where a function sends each input, as in x maps to x squared.

binomial-coefficient.context: A small n above a small k inside tall parentheses, the binomial coefficient read n choose k. Counts the ways to pick k items from n, and gives the numbers in Pascal's triangle.

basis-point.context: A percent-style sign with one ring above a slash and three rings below, the per ten thousand sign. One basis point is a hundredth of a percent, common in interest rates and finance.

system-of-equations.context: Two short stacked equations joined on the left by a tall curly brace, a system of equations. Used in algebra lessons for simultaneous equations solved together.

quadratic-equation.context: An x squared term inside the U of a parabola, standing for a quadratic equation and its graph. Used for algebra topics, polynomial solvers and math homework help.

dot-product.context: Two vector letters u and v, each under a small arrow, with a bold dot between them. The dot product multiplies two vectors into a single number.

function-composition.context: The letters f and g joined by a small hollow ring, the composition of two functions. Means apply g first and then f to the result.

transpose-matrix.context: A bracketed matrix with a small raised letter T at its top right, the transpose of a matrix. Transposing swaps rows and columns, used in linear algebra and data work.

imaginary-unit.context: The letter i beside the square root of minus one, the imaginary unit. Used for complex numbers in algebra, electrical engineering and signal processing.

parabola.context: A U-shaped curve on x and y axes with a dot at its lowest point, a parabola and its vertex. Shows quadratic graphs, projectile paths and the shape of reflector dishes.

ellipse-foci.context: A wide ellipse with its two foci marked and lines from each focus to one point on the curve. Explains how an ellipse is drawn and why planets follow elliptical orbits.

unit-circle.context: A circle centred on crossed axes, with one radius to a point on the edge and its angle marked. The unit circle is the basis of sine, cosine and radians in trigonometry.

polar-grid.context: A quarter of a polar grid: arcs around an origin, rays at set angles and one plotted point. Used for polar coordinates, radar style plots and navigation bearings.

three-d-axes.context: Three arrows from one origin, pointing up, right and diagonally toward the viewer, the x, y and z axes. Used for 3D coordinates, modeling software and physics diagrams.

slope-triangle.context: A rising line on a pair of axes with a small right triangle under it, showing rise over run. Used to teach slope, gradient and rate of change in linear graphs.

sierpinski-triangle.context: A triangle broken into nine smaller triangles with the middle spaces left empty, two levels of the Sierpinski triangle. A classic example of a fractal and of self similar patterns.

koch-snowflake.context: A snowflake outline built from triangles, with smaller triangular bumps on every edge, the Koch snowflake. A classic fractal with a finite area and an ever growing perimeter.

mandelbrot-set.context: The outline of the Mandelbrot set, a heart-shaped cardioid with a round bulb on its left and small buds around it. Known from fractal art, chaos theory and complex dynamics.

fractal-tree.context: A tree whose trunk splits into two branches that each split again, a simple binary fractal tree. Used to show recursion, branching growth and tree data structures.

trefoil-knot.context: A closed three-lobed loop that crosses over and under itself three times, the trefoil knot. It is the simplest true knot and a standard example in knot theory and topology.

tesseract.context: A small square nested in a larger one with their corners joined, the usual drawing of a tesseract. A tesseract is a four-dimensional hypercube, a cube extended into one more dimension.

octahedron.context: Two square pyramids joined base to base, a diamond-shaped solid with its front edges drawn. The octahedron is one of the five Platonic solids and the shape of an eight-sided die.

dodecahedron.context: A solid of twelve pentagon faces, drawn as a central pentagon ringed by five more inside a ten-sided outline. One of the five Platonic solids and the shape of a twelve-sided die.

icosahedron.context: A solid of twenty triangle faces, drawn as a central triangle surrounded by more triangles in a hexagonal outline. One of the five Platonic solids and the shape of a twenty-sided die.

frustum.context: A cone with its top sliced off flat, with an elliptical top and base and the hidden back edge shown dashed. Used for frustum volume problems and the view frustum in 3D graphics.

cube-net.context: Six squares arranged in a cross, the flat net that folds up into a cube. Used in geometry lessons on surface area, nets and folding 3D shapes.

hexagonal-prism.context: An upright prism with hexagonal top and bottom, drawn in perspective with its front faces. Used for geometry of solids, pencils, nuts and crystal shapes.

hemisphere.context: Half a sphere resting on its flat round base, with the hidden back of the rim shown dashed. Used for volume and surface area problems and for dome shapes.

circle-circumference.context: A circle with a curved arrow running around its outside edge, the circumference. Stands for the distance around a circle, equal to pi times the diameter.

sector-of-circle.context: A circle with one pie slice between two radii filled in, a sector. Used for sector area, arc length and central angle problems in geometry.

inscribed-angle.context: A circle with two chords that meet at a point on its edge, with the angle between them filled in. Illustrates the inscribed angle theorem and other circle theorems.

heptagon.context: A regular polygon with seven equal sides and corners. Used in geometry lessons and as a shape for badges, coins and tiles.

decagon.context: A regular polygon with ten equal sides and corners. Used in geometry lessons and as a shape for badges, tiles and frames.

angle-bisector.context: An angle made of two rays with a dashed ray between them that splits it into two equal marked parts. Used in compass and straightedge constructions and triangle geometry.

perpendicular-bisector.context: A line segment with marked endpoints crossed at its midpoint by a dashed line, with a right angle mark. Used in geometry constructions and for finding points equally far from two points.

line-of-symmetry.context: A leaf shape split into two mirror-image halves by a dashed vertical line. Used to teach reflection symmetry and mirror lines in art, design and geometry.

rotational-symmetry.context: A three-bladed pinwheel with a curved arrow sweeping around it, showing rotational symmetry. The shape looks the same after each one third turn.

tessellation-pattern.context: Hexagon tiles that fit together with no gaps inside a square frame, a tessellation. Used for tiling patterns, honeycomb grids and geometry lessons.

sine-cosine-waves.context: Two waves on the same line, a solid sine wave and a dashed cosine wave shifted by a quarter period. Used for trigonometry, oscillation, phase shift and signal topics.
